note.explanation: Food is transported through phloem. In most plants, it travels as sucrose from a source, where food is available, to a sink, where food is used or stored. Loading sucrose at the source draws water into the phloem and raises its pressure. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water leaves the phloem, lowering its pressure. This pressure difference drives the flow of food.
examples: A mesophyll cell in a leaf can be a source; a growing root tip can be a sink.
A root storing food can be a source when it supplies food, or a sink when it receives food for storage.
note.checkAnswer: Food moves in phloem from higher pressure at the source towards lower pressure at the sink.
note.simple: Think of food flowing through phloem from where it is supplied to where it is needed or stored. Water pressure helps push it along.
note.checkQuestion: Why does food flow from the source towards the sink?
note.title: How food moves through a plant
steps: At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes.
Water enters the sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The fluid pressure rises at the source, pushing food solution towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded and water moves into the xylem by osmosis.
The pressure is lower at the sink, so food flows in bulk from the higher-pressure source towards it.
note.answer: Food moves through phloem from a source to a sink because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
written.finalAnswer: At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes using energy from companion cells. Water enters the sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis, raising fluid pressure. Food solution flows towards the sink. At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded and water moves into the xylem by osmosis, lowering fluid pressure. The higher pressure at the source than at the sink causes food to flow in bulk towards the sink.

modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

explain.title: What is translocation?
explain.body: “We know that inside the plant body, food is transported from one part to the other through phloem tissue.” This movement of food is called translocation. In most plants, glucose is converted into sucrose for transport.

explain.title: Sources and sinks
explain.body: “The sources include photosynthetic tissues (e.g. mesophyll of leaves) and storage tissues (e.g. roots). Sinks include the sites of food utilization (e.g. growing tips of roots and stems) and the storage tissues.” A source supplies food; a sink uses or stores it.

explain.title: Pressure flow mechanism
explain.body: “The mechanism of the transport of food in plants is called pressure flow mechanism.” At the source, sucrose loading causes water to enter the sieve tubes by osmosis, raising fluid pressure.

explain.title: Food moves towards the sink
explain.body: “Due to higher fluid pressure at the source than the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.” At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water moves into the xylem, lowering the pressure.

explain.title: Xylem and phloem differ
explain.body: “Xylem is a one-way passage for water and salts (from roots to leaves). Phloem is a two-way passage for food.” Food direction depends on supply and demand at sources and sinks.

mistakes: Do not say that food travels in xylem; food is transported through phloem.
Do not describe phloem as one-way; it is a two-way passage, with movement depending on sources and sinks.
Do not mix up active transport and osmosis: sucrose is actively transported, while water moves by osmosis.
Do not say water enters the sieve tubes at the sink; at the sink, water moves from sieve tubes into the xylem.
Do not leave out the pressure difference: higher pressure at the source drives bulk flow towards the sink.
